prompt: In the ProductList/ProductCard/Price example, how does data move between components?
choices: One direction, top to bottom: a parent passes data down to children as props, and a child cannot reach back up to change a prop it was given
Bidirectionally: a child component can freely reassign a prop it receives, and the change flows back up to the parent automatically
Siblings share data directly with each other without going through any parent component
Props are only used for styling; actual data must always go through useState in every component

prompt: A component has `let countDirect = 0;` declared outside the component function, and a button's onClick does `countDirect += 1; console.log(countDirect);`. The console shows the number climbing on each click, but the number displayed in the button's label never changes. Why?
choices: Only calls to a useState setter schedule a re-render; mutating a plain variable outside React's state gives React no signal that anything changed, so it never re-renders to show the new value
React automatically re-renders every component once per second regardless of state changes, so the label will eventually update on its own
console.log calls secretly block React from re-rendering until the page is refreshed
Button elements in React cannot display dynamic text, only static strings written directly in JSX

prompt: Given `const [items, setItems] = useState(['a', 'b']);`, why does `items.push('c'); setItems(items);` fail to trigger a re-render, while `setItems([...items, 'c'])` works correctly?
choices: push() only works on arrays of numbers, never on arrays of strings

setItems(items) passes the same array reference as before (since push mutates in place), so React sees no change and skips re-rendering; the spread version creates a new array reference, which React detects as a real change
React re-renders on every setItems call regardless of the argument, so both versions behave identically
setItems can only accept arrays with exactly two elements

prompt: A useEffect with an empty dependency array (`[]`) sets up a setInterval that calls `setCount(count + 1)` every second, reading `count` from the surrounding component. The displayed count jumps from 0 to 1 and then never changes again. What's the root cause?
choices: setInterval is broken in React and should never be used inside useEffect
The effect runs once at mount, and the interval's callback closes over the `count` value from that single run (0) forever, so it always computes setCount(0 + 1); it never sees any later count
Empty dependency arrays are invalid syntax and silently stop the effect from running at all
setCount can only be called once per component's lifetime

prompt: What fixes the stale-closure interval bug from the previous question, while keeping the effect's dependency array empty?
choices: Replacing setCount(count + 1) with the functional updater form, setCount((prevCount) => prevCount + 1), so React supplies the actual current state when the update runs instead of relying on the closure's captured value
Adding a second, identical setInterval call right after the first one
Removing the cleanup function that calls clearInterval
Switching from useState to a plain global variable declared outside the component

prompt: In the UserProfile fetch-on-mount example, the effect's cleanup function sets a local `ignore` flag to true. What problem does this solve?
choices: It prevents the component from ever fetching data a second time, no matter what

It stops a slow response for an old userId from overwriting the component's state after userId has already changed to something newer, by having the old effect's callbacks check `ignore` before calling setState
It is required by JavaScript syntax any time fetch() is used inside useEffect, regardless of behavior
It makes the fetch request complete faster by canceling unrelated network traffic

prompt: In the GithubLookup component, why does the catch block check `if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;` before setting an error message?
choices: Because AbortError means the GitHub API itself returned a 500 server error
Because that check is only there for logging purposes and has no effect on behavior

Because an AbortError happens when the component's own cleanup function deliberately cancelled the request (e.g., the user typed a new username before the old request finished), so it isn't a real failure and shouldn't be shown to the user as one
Because fetch() throws an AbortError every time a request succeeds, so it must be filtered out

prompt: In the React Router example, what does the `end` prop on `<NavLink to="/" end>` do?
choices: It deletes the route once the user navigates away from it
It makes the link require two clicks to navigate instead of one

Without it, '/' would match as a prefix of every other path (like '/about'), so the Home link would stay visually marked as active even while viewing other pages; `end` restricts the match to the exact path
It disables client-side navigation for that specific link, forcing a full page reload
